purpose: Turn a force at a fixed application point and follow its perpendicular component into signed torque about the pivot.
meaning: The torque of a force about a chosen pivot is the cross product of its position vector with the force vector. Its perpendicular lever arm is the distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. In the displayed plane, the signed normal component distinguishes turning senses, while its magnitude measures the turning effect without a sign.

definition.setting: A planar force applied at a stated distance from a fixed pivot in a right-handed coordinate frame.

signature.F_x: Force component along the fixed x axis.
signature.r⃗: Position vector from pivot to application point.
signature.r⃗×F⃗: Torque vector formed from the ordered cross product.

conditions: The position vector and force vector use a fixed right-handed frame. The application point is r metres along positive x, with 0≤r≤2 m; the force magnitude satisfies 0≤F≤20 N.

The construction setting θ ranges from −180 to 180 degrees relative to the positive x axis. For nonzero position and force vectors it is the directed angle from the position vector toward the force. If either vector is zero, the setting does not give that zero vector a direction.

The signed perpendicular force is F⊥=F sinθ. The actual moment arm d⊥=r|sinθ| is the perpendicular distance to the force line of action when the force is nonzero; it generally differs from r. At zero force, the construction still supplies d⊥ but the zero force vector has no distinguished line of action.
The signed component τ_z=rF sinθ is in N·m. Positive z points out of the page and positive planar torque is counterclockwise. A zero torque has no distinguished normal direction.
Torque is a turning effect about a selected pivot. Although N·m has the same dimensional form as a joule, this torque value is not energy or work.
definition.domain_notes: The metre distance and Newton force have separate drawing scales. Arrows over r and F denote the position and force vectors; plain r and F in the scalar component formula denote their stated magnitudes. The model evaluates torque for the stated geometry; it does not integrate motion or account for friction, inertia or a force needed to open a real door.
definition.proof_status: Definition-level sources and original restricted-family arguments; independent review pending.

grammar.formation_rule: Let r be the nonnegative pivot-to-application distance and F the nonnegative force magnitude. In the fixed plane the position vector is (r,0,0) m and the force vector is (F cosθ,F sinθ,0) N. Their cross product has signed component τ_z=rF sinθ. The perpendicular lever arm is d⊥=r|sinθ| and the torque magnitude is |τ_z|=F d⊥.
grammar.precedence: Resolve the force’s signed perpendicular component F⊥=F sinθ before multiplying by the application distance r. Take absolute value when reading torque magnitude or perpendicular lever-arm distance.

properties.claim: The largest torque magnitude for fixed r and F occurs at a right angle.
properties.conditions: Keep r,F≥0 fixed in the displayed planar family.
properties.derivation: |τ_z|=rF|sinθ|≤rF, with equality at ±90° when both magnitudes are positive.

properties.claim: Application distance and moment arm generally differ.
properties.conditions: Use an oblique nonzero force and nonzero position vector.
properties.derivation: At 30°, d⊥=r/2, while r remains the full pivot-to-application distance.
properties.status: author-derived for stated conditions; independent mathematical review pending

properties.claim: Reversing the signed right angle reverses torque while preserving its magnitude.
properties.conditions: Use the same pivot, application distance and force magnitude.
properties.derivation: The sine changes sign and its absolute value remains one.
properties.status: author-derived for stated conditions; independent mathematical review pending

prompts.prompt: Is r always the perpendicular lever arm?
prompts.answer: No. At 30° the perpendicular moment arm is r sin30°=r/2. At 90° it equals r.

prompts.prompt: Does the computed torque tell how fast a real door rotates?
prompts.answer: No. The module evaluates the turning effect of the stated force; motion needs additional information such as inertia and other forces.
